pull.title: net: require a dedicated bind for automatic Tor
pull.body:
**Problem:** When the automatic onion service has no dedicated `-bind=<addr>=onion`, Tor forwards incoming connections to the first normal P2P bind. A wildcard onion bind also fails to identify incoming Tor connections. In either case, network classification is incorrect and Tor peers may inherit permissions granted to the Tor daemon's IP address.

**Fix:** Refuse startup when `-listenonion` is enabled and an explicit `-bind` configuration lacks a dedicated, non-wildcard onion bind or includes a wildcard onion bind, following [the recommendation in #34892](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34892#issuecomment-5541662236). Users should add a specific `-bind=<addr>=onion` or set `-listenonion=0`.

Because `-listenonion` is enabled by default when listening, existing configurations with only a normal `-bind` must also be updated. Nodes without explicit `-bind` options retain the default dedicated onion listener.

Concept ACK

`0.0.0.0` is the default for `-bind` itself, and `-bind=0.0.0.0:8334=onion` passes the new check while tagging nothing. `addr_bind` comes from `GetBindAddress` on the accepted socket, so what `CreateNodeFromAcceptedSocket` compares against `m_onion_binds` is the concrete address the peer reached.

Same node, same arriving address, same `-whitelist`. With `-bind=0.0.0.0:P=onion` the inbound peer is classified by its IP network in `getpeerinfo` and keeps its `noban`. Spelling that same address out instead of the wildcard gives `onion` with no permissions. `[::]` is classified the same way, and either wildcard is what reaches Tor as the `ADD_ONION` target.

Rejecting a wildcard onion bind would close that. Naming `127.0.0.1:8334=onion` in the message would only make it less likely. Is the first one in scope here?

> Rejecting a wildcard onion bind would close that. Naming 127.0.0.1:8334=onion in the message would only make it less likely. Is the first one in scope here?

Thanks , added a wildcard-bind check and test (added you as coauthor), but I’d appreciate a second look from e.g. @vasild who has more experience with this part of the networking code than I do.

Keep in mind that when running in a container, it is considered best practise to bind to `0.0.0.0` / `[::]` rather than a specific IP. That is because most container engines (e.g. Docker) use dynamic IPs.

The issue that `0.0.0.0` / `[::]` are unsuitable to pass via Tor control should imho be solved by a second configuration option, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/25094.

init: reject shared and wildcard Tor binds

Tor peers arriving through shared or wildcard binds may be classified by IP and inherit address-based whitelist permissions.
Reject those configurations when the automatic onion service is enabled.

Because `-listenonion` is enabled by default when listening, existing plain `-bind` configurations also need a dedicated onion bind or `-listenonion=0`, even if they do not use Tor.

Co-authored-by: Vasil Dimov <vd@FreeBSD.org>

since #34892 was closed in favour of this PR (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34892#issuecomment-5577081511), i think it makes sense to add a `fixes #33458` in the the PR description so that the issue can be closed on merge because this PR actually resolves the issue

> Because -listenonion is enabled by default when listening, existing configurations with only a normal -bind must also be updated. 

I'm not sure about this approach. So any existing deployment that has a single bind, which I think is a common configuration, will now fail to start? That seems harsh to me. How about falling back to the default onion bind if no explicit one is given? Maybe I'm missing something, but wouldn't that match more closely with what would be expected to happen with a default on feature?

> So any existing deployment that has a single bind, which I think is a common configuration

Shouldn't be because that is flawed because then incoming IP and Tor cannot be distinguished. But I have no idea how widespread it is.

> will now fail to start?

Right.

> That seems harsh to me.

I agree, it is.

Like a wake up call "fix your config!"

> How about falling back to the default onion bind if no explicit one is given? Maybe I'm missing something, but wouldn't that match more closely with what would be expected to happen with a default on feature?

Note that then there is no way to disable the Tor bind. Right now we have:
* by default both IP and Tor bind (if the user specifies no options)
* if the user specifies only IP bind then we bind for IP only
* if the user specifies both IP bind and Tor bind then we bind for both.

I think that is logical and is a natural way to disable the Tor bind. By IP bind I mean `-bind=` and by Tor bind I mean `-bind=...=onion`.

I agree it is harsh. I think it is acceptable though. But if others find it unacceptable, then it is unacceptable. What other ways might be, hmm...

So, the problem is if `-listenonion=1` and only `-bind=` is used without `-bind=...=onion`. Then we tell the Tor daemon to forward incoming Tor connections to our normal bind and we cannot distinguish those from incoming IP connections.

Some ideas, if the current approach seems unacceptable:

* Log a startup warning and still end up in a state where IP and Tor incomings cannot be distinguished. A warning in the GUI as a pop up window will be noticed, but `bitcoind` users with only a warning in the log will probably miss it.

* Brick only the Tor listening service. That is - allow start but refuse to create the Tor listening service and log a warning periodically, like:

> -listenonion is enabled but the Tor listening service was not created because there is no separate -bind=...=onion. To accept incoming Tor connections either remove the explicit -bind= which you have used (that will enable the default -bind=127.0.0.1:8334=onion) or add an explicit -bind=...=onion to your config.

Might result the node operating in semi-degraded state for a long time before the user notices they have no incoming Tor connections and starts investigating. I still like more the refuse-to-start approach because it is obvious.

The root problem here is that there are two options that have to be set together: if `-listenonion` is set, then `-bind=...=onion` must also be set. And we are trying to handle the cases in which the later is not set. That is a bad interface.

**A good interface is impossible to misuse.**

So, what about another idea: the name of the option `-listenonion` is very confusing. I have always wished to do something about it ever since I grasped what it does. What it does is to automatically create the Tor service. It has nothing to do with listening, as in `-bind`. We might accept incoming Tor connections without it as well, if the Tor service is statically configured inside the Tor daemon, in `torrc`.

So, what about replacing `-listenonion` with `-bind=addr:port=onionauto`? Note that in order to enable the auto Tor service creation, now one must specify a bind address and port. It is bundled together, impossible to misuse. Currently one can enable auto Tor service without specifying the listening address:port and that is a problem.

old | new
---|---
`-listenonion=0` | don't specify `-bind=addr:port=onionauto`
`-listenonion=1` | `-bind=addr:port=onionauto`

The old default is as if `-listenonion=1 -bind=0.0.0.0:8333 -bind=127.0.0.1:8334=onion` were given. The new one will be as if `-bind=0.0.0.0:8333 -bind=127.0.0.1:8334=onionauto` were given.

What about the problematic case where the user has only explicitly set `-bind=addr:port` and has inherited the default `-listenonion=1` (and thus cannot distinguish incoming IP from Tor)? In the new variant with only an explicit `-bind=addr:port` and without an explicit `-bind=addr:port=onionauto` the Tor service will not be created.

> Shouldn't be because that is flawed because then incoming IP and Tor cannot be distinguished. But I have no idea how widespread it is.

Doing a cursory search, singular binds in general seem very common, it's even on the bitcoin wiki. I did find a couple of deployment configurations that don't include tor and set a single bind ([1](https://github.com/bitaps-com/bitcoin-core), [2](https://github.com/fooock/bitcoind-ansible/blob/main/templates/bitcoin.conf.j2)). 

> Brick only the Tor listening service. That is - allow start but refuse to create the Tor listening service and log a warning periodically, like:

I don't see why we would necessarily have to brick it. Wouldn't using the current default bind if not onion bind is provided just continue working for most deployments?

> Wouldn't using the current default bind if not onion bind is provided just continue working for most deployments?

That is to ditch this PR? Then leave the problem it tries to resolve opened, from the OP:

> Problem: When the automatic onion service has no dedicated -bind=<addr>=onion, Tor forwards incoming connections to the first normal P2P bind. ... network classification is incorrect and Tor peers may inherit permissions granted to the Tor daemon's IP address.

FWIW I considered this fine (to not be able to distinguish incoming Tor from IP), but I didn't think it would be widespread. It is a misconfiguration. And then AIs came and told us this this dangerous and I kind of agree to some extent...

> That is to ditch this PR? Then leave the problem it tries to resolve opened, from the OP:

I'm not suggesting doing nothing. Maybe I'm not quite following the actual problems, but what I'm suggesting is basically along the lines of adding `-bind=127.0.0.1:<-port+1>=onion` internally whenever a non-onion bind at port is detected in combination with `-listenonion` and no onion bind is given. Could also combine this with a warning that they should set their onion bind explicitly. I'm also not really sold whether to call this a misconfiguration, or a bug on our side.

Requested comments on [IRC](https://bitcoin-irc.chaincode.com/bitcoin-core-dev/2026-11-13#1274242):

> RFC for #36170: Tor peers sharing a normal bind can inherit IP-based whitelist permissions.
Should we add a default onion listener (see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36170#issuecomment-6823929169), refuse startup (current PR), or warn and skip service creation?
Refusal affects non-Tor setups because -listenonion defaults on - adding a listener changes explicit bind behavior (and maybe risks port conflicts).

Wonder if we can navigate this issue through only failing during startup if:
`-listenonion` AND `-bind=IP` AND `-whitelist` has been set.
E.g., if this *only* is an issue when differing permissions are set for different IPs *and* adjusting permissions is not common, then this should catch the cases we worry about, while letting harmless & common cases continue.

But maybe I'm missing some detail, I've just had a first look.
(This idea was also communicated out of band with l0rinc).

comments.body:
```suggestion
        return InitError(_("The automatic Tor onion service requires a dedicated onion bind. Use a specific address such as -bind=127.0.0.1:<port>=onion, or disable the service with -listenonion=0."));
```

With this PR the automatic Tor service requires a dedicated bind, always, unconditionally. Not only "when -bind is set".

To clarify - if the user did not set `-bind`, then the defaults do provide both `-bind` and `-bind=...=onion`.

Isn't this check redundant? Seems to be the same as the added check in `AppInitParameterInteraction()`. Better have just one. I prefer this one because it uses `connOptions.onion_binds`. The other one manually "parses" the arguments and checks for `=onion` suffix which is redundant with the code that sets `connOptions.onion_binds`. That is, if `=onion` would have to be changed to e.g. to support case insensitive match, then it would have to be changed in two places, not nice.

This message is technically not correct. If wildcard address is used, incoming Tor connections will still be identified just fine. For example: `-bind=1.2.3.4:8333 -bind=0.0.0.0:8334=onion` - anything that arrives on port `8334` will be correctly identified as incoming Tor.

The problem, however, is that `0.0.0.0:8334` in addition to being used for binding and classifying connections is also used to instruct the Tor daemon to forward incoming connections to it. And telling the Tor daemon to forward connections to `0.0.0.0:8334` is ill.

So, maybe something like: "The automatic Tor onion service cannot use a wildcard onion bind because the Tor daemon wouldn't be able to forward incoming connections to us. Use a specific address such as `-bind=127.0.0.1:<port>=onion`, or disable the service with `-listenonion=0`."

Or just: "The automatic Tor onion service cannot use a wildcard onion bind. Use a specific address such as `-bind=127.0.0.1:<port>=onion`, or disable the service with `-listenonion=0`."

comments.body:
Further clarification (thanks for double checking this after an offline chat):

* Indeed shared binds cannot distinguish incoming Tor vs direct connections. E.g. if we bind on `1.2.3.4:8333` and accept incoming Tor and incoming direct connections on that address and port then we can't distinguish, obviously.

* If we use a wildcard bind for Tor, e.g. `-bind=0.0.0.0:8334=onion`, then the problem is slightly different. I got this wrong initially, thanks for correcting me. The wildcard will bind on all addresses of the machine, e.g. `127.0.0.1:8334`, `1.2.3.4:8334`, `5.6.7.8:8334` and there will be no overlap between those and the direct connections `1.2.3.4:8333`. So far so good, but when an incoming Tor connection arrives, we will then compare the address it arrived on e.g. `5.6.7.8:8334` to whatever was given to `-bind` which is `0.0.0.0:8334` and that will not match :bomb:. So the connection will be wrongly not considered as an incoming Tor connection. In theory, if we want to fix this:

https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/6301d464f72d2752867c974e747f7a78b4f8322f/src/net.cpp#L1791

then we would have to tweak that comparison to "if there is an entry in `m_onion_bind` that is a wildcard and the port matches to the port in `addr_bind`, then consider they are equal. I think that is unnecessary.

* `s/Tor-forwarded connections/incoming Tor connections/`
